question.problem: At which points on the surface $z=8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =24{x}^{2}-12y \\  & =12(2{x}^{2}-y) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =-12x+3{y}^{2} \\  & =3({y}^{2}-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨12(2{x}^{2}-y),\,3({y}^{2}-4x),\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}12(2{x}^{2}-y)=0 \\ 3({y}^{2}-4x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=2{x}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3({(2{x}^{2})}^{2}-4x) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{4}-4x & =0 \\ 4x({x}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions of the last equation are $x=0,1.$ So, we have two cases.

- For $x=0,$ we have 

$$
y=2({0}^{2})=0.
$$

Now, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({0}^{3})-12(0)(0)+{0}^{3}+1=1.
$$

So, our first point is $(0,0,1).$

- For $x=1,$ we have 

$$
y=2({1}^{2})=2.
$$

Now, substituting $x=1$ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({1}^{3})-12(1)(2)+{2}^{3}+1=-7.
$$

So, our second point is $(1,2,-7).$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,2,-7).$
